blocks.text: I can appreciate the structure of patterns and sequences.
We will look at two kinds of number pattern and find out how each one works.

items.title: Constant {additive} pattern
items.sub: the same number is added each time

items.title: Constant {multiplicative} pattern
items.sub: the same number multiplies each time

blocks.text: Tap the word to see what it means.

items.def: A sequence is a succession of objects, diagrams or values usually formed according to a rule.

blocks.text: Look at this sequence of numbers. The dots mean it carries on in the same pattern.

blocks.label: What do you notice?
blocks.text: If you add 3 to the previous number, you get the next number. It is the beginning of the 3 times table.
Here is a section of the 2 times table: 34, 36, 38, 40, …

items: Each number goes up by 2. The rule is add 2.
The next number after 40 is 40 + 2 = 42.
To go backwards we do the inverse. The number before 34 is 34 − 2 = 32.

blocks.text: Multiplication tables are sequences with a constant {additive} pattern: we add the same value each time.
Successive numbers (numbers next to each other) in the 2 times table have a difference of 2. In the 3 times table the difference is 3, and in the 4 times table it is 4.

blocks.q: Which of these is a section of the 8 times table?
blocks.why: The 8 times table goes up by 8 each time: 48 + 8 = 56, 56 + 8 = 64, 64 + 8 = 72.

blocks.text: To find what a sequence adds each time, subtract two numbers that are next to each other: later number − earlier number.

items: 14, 19, …  gives 19 − 14 = 5, so the rule is add 5.
To find the previous number, do the inverse: 14 − 5 = 9.

blocks.text: If the pattern is constant, any two neighbouring numbers give the same difference. Written methods, like column subtraction, are always fine to use.
Look at 23, 19, … The difference is 19 − 23 = −4, so we are adding −4 each time.

items: Adding −4 is the same as subtracting 4.
Next number: 19 − 4 = 15.
Previous number: 23 + 4 = 27 (the inverse).

blocks.text: Forming a sequence by adding a negative value makes a {decreasing} sequence.
Does 27, 41, 57, … have a constant additive pattern?

blocks.label: Tap to check
blocks.text: No. 41 − 27 = 14 but 57 − 41 = 16. The same value has not been added each time.
Now try 9, 19, 29, 39, 49, … These are not the 9 times table, but they do have a constant additive pattern: we add 10 each time.
Times tables are just one type of additive sequence. They are not the only type.

blocks.q: Is the pattern constant additive or constant multiplicative? Put each sequence in the correct column.

blocks.text: Some sequences follow a rule other than adding the same value each time. Some follow a constant multiplicative pattern: we multiply by the same number each time.
In 2, 4, 8, 16, … each number is multiplied by 2 to get the next one.
To find the multiplier, divide a number by the one before it. Take 6, 18, 54, …

items: 54 ÷ 18 = 3 (the same, so the pattern is constant)
The multiplier is 3. The next number is 54 × 3 = 162.

blocks.text: Sequences can have decimal or fractional multipliers. Take 80, 20, 5, …

items: Multiplier: 20 ÷ 80 = 1/4 (or 0.25). Check: 5 ÷ 20 = 1/4 too.
Next number: 5 × 1/4 = 1.25.
Previous number: 80 ÷ 1/4 = 320 (the inverse of multiplying is dividing).

blocks.text: Multiplying a positive number by a value between 0 and 1 gives a smaller number, so a sequence like 27, 9, 3, 1, … decreases.
Sequences can have negative multipliers. Take 4, −20, 100, …

items: Next number: 100 × (−5) = −500.
Previous number: 4 ÷ (−5) = −0.8.

blocks.text: With a negative multiplier the numbers switch between positive and negative.

blocks.label: Is 1, −1, 1, −1, … additive?
blocks.text: No. We add −2, then add 2, so the amount added is not constant. Each value is multiplied by −1 to get the next value, so it is a constant multiplicative pattern.

blocks.q: Each sequence has a constant multiplicative pattern. What is the multiplier?
Choose the next number in each sequence.

items: A sequence is a succession of objects, diagrams or values usually formed according to a rule.
Multiplication tables are examples of sequences. Their difference is the number of the table.
In a constant additive sequence, the difference between neighbouring numbers is always the same. Later − earlier finds it.
In a constant multiplicative sequence, there is a specific multiplier. Later ÷ earlier finds it.
Multipliers can be decimals, fractions or negative. A negative multiplier switches between positive and negative numbers.
Writing the sequence out with arrows and using written methods helps with larger numbers.

flashcards.back: A sequence is a succession of objects, diagrams or values usually formed according to a rule.

flashcards.front: Multiplication tables are an example of what kind of sequence?
flashcards.back: A sequence with a constant additive pattern. The 4 times table goes up by 4 each time.

flashcards.front: How do you find the difference in a constant additive sequence?
flashcards.back:
Subtract the earlier number from the later number that is next to it.

19 − 14 = 5

flashcards.front: How do you find the previous number in an additive sequence that adds 5?
What does adding a negative number, such as +(−4), do to a sequence?
flashcards.back: It makes a decreasing sequence. Adding −4 is the same as subtracting 4.

flashcards.front: Does 27, 41, 57, … have a constant additive pattern?
flashcards.back: No. 41 − 27 = 14 but 57 − 41 = 16, so the same value is not added each time.

flashcards.front: How do you find the multiplier in a constant multiplicative sequence?
flashcards.back:
Divide a number by the number before it.

In 6, 18, 54, … the multiplier is 18 ÷ 6 = 3.

flashcards.front: Find the next number in 6, 18, 54, … (constant multiplicative)
How do you find the previous number in a multiplicative sequence?
flashcards.back: Do the inverse: divide by the multiplier.

flashcards.front: Can a multiplier be a fraction or a decimal?
What happens to the signs in a sequence with a negative multiplier?
flashcards.back:
The numbers switch between positive and negative.

4, −20, 100, −500, …
Multiply by −1 each time. It is not additive because we add −2, then add 2.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Checking understanding of sequences
worksheet.instructions: Each sequence has either a constant additive pattern or a constant multiplicative pattern. Work out the difference or the multiplier first, then answer. Type a minus sign as - and write decimals with a decimal point.

questions.prompt: A sequence has a constant additive pattern and starts 14, 19, … What is the 6th number in the sequence?
questions.explanation: Each step adds 19 − 14 = 5. There are 5 steps from the 1st to the 6th number: 14 + 5 × 5 = 39.

questions.prompt: The sequence 258, 584, 910, … has a constant additive pattern. What number is added each time?
What is the next number in the constant additive sequence 7.8, 9.2, 10.6, …?
A sequence has a constant additive pattern and starts 31, 26, … What is the next number?
The constant additive sequence …, ?, 12.7, 13.3, … has a number missing before 12.7. What is it?
questions.explanation: The difference is 13.3 − 12.7 = 0.6. To go back, subtract 0.6: 12.7 − 0.6 = 12.1.

questions.prompt: What is the next number in the constant multiplicative sequence 2, 8, 32, …?
The sequence 24, 96, … has a constant multiplicative pattern. What is the multiplier?
What is the next number in the constant multiplicative sequence 1000, 100, 10, …?
What is the next number in the constant multiplicative sequence 80, 20, 5, …? Give your answer as a decimal.
What is the next number in the constant multiplicative sequence 1, −3, 9, −27, …?
